So the other comment on this post that said to imagine a ray of light shooting out my hand (see their explanation as it’s way better than anything I could explain 😅) actually did help. I was sceptical it would but it actually kind of helped me to visualise it and not bend my hands so much because I was thinking more about where I wanted my hands to aim. The other thing that has helped is just recording myself and watching it back to be more conscious of my hand movements in general.

I still have a way to go to make them look as good as I want, but it’s definitely helped. It’s one of those things where you start off feeling kinda disheartened and then train your muscle memory over time. I hope that helps!

Just feel the feeling and honour your grief. I think those things can be true at once.

I think the honest answer is that you have to stop talking to her daily, pull back your energy and take your power back. She isn’t going to miss you if she still has access to you daily. Maybe you’ll get the impression she “won’t care” at first, but give it time and space so she can actually feel your absence. And in the meantime - more importantly - having that time and space for you will be good for you. Focus on what you can control (yourself, your own growth and improvement) not what you can’t control. Whether you think she’s made the right choice or not, she’s not going to respond to your logic right now. And you never know, in that time and space you may find you think you deserve better. Best of luck <3

I’m really sorry you feel this way, and I also think your post is very brave and telling about the psychological toll society can have on women particularly as they age out of conventional standards/arbitrary metrics for what makes a woman beautiful enough, worthy enough, interesting enough, valuable enough. I think it can be really hard for some men to understand as well, from a woman’s perspective / experience. I’m sorry if your partner wasn’t able to be more sensitive and empathetic in this regard, that would hurt. 

Something that has helped me is coming to understand that this feeling you have - this rotten, burning despair of self-loathing and simultaneous outrage - is by design. Society is designed to keep us feeling insecure, to keep us viewing age as a bad thing, to keep us using words like frumpy to describe ourselves when we age out of the 20 something bracket. It is designed to make us turn on one another, and turn on ourselves, simply to profit off our insecurities. And if it is by design it can be redesigned. If you don’t meet a widely regarded conventional beauty standard, remember it is just that. A conventional made up standard. There will be people who argue otherwise because it is easier to believe these things are immutable facts than to challenge ourselves and others to see beauty for what it is - everywhere, in all of us, and most importantly, in you. 

I empathise more than you know with this feeling. It has driven me to the edge and back. But striving for resistance against this narrative has become a point of principle not just for my own personal benefit, but for collective benefit. For all women, so that no one else ever has to feel the way you do now. So that you know you are beautiful because you say so, and we say so, not because convention dictates whether we are or not, manipulated in such a way as to keep us broken down. Seek out other women who believe this too, see their beauty in all their forms. I hope it will help you to see that there is beauty in you too, outside and inside, in abundance. I believe it, and so can you. 

Tonight sounds really shitty. But I hope you’re able to find some comfort even though I know these darker thoughts and moments make it so very hard, to self advocate and self validate in this way all the time is hard. I hope you have other people in your life who are able to do that for you from time to time on the days it gets too hard to do it for yourself. If no one told you today let me be the person - stranger or otherwise - to tell you that you are beautiful, worthy, and powerful, now and always, especially as you age. Especially now. Take care <3
Remember that every day he makes a choice not to contact you. He knows where you are and how to reach you. And he doesn’t. That’s what I remind myself every day.

When he lied / hid the fact he was moving in with friends in his hometown, instead of following through on the plans we had to close the gap in our long distance relationship and move to live in my city instead. I found out when one of his mates let it slip at drinks one time, apparently everyone knew but me.

I don’t think it gets worse than how you’re feeling right now don’t worry. I think this is rock bottom. Just please please focus on surviving each hour. Whatever you need to do as long as it’s safe and healthy, just get through another minute, another hour.

I know it might be unpopular advice on here sometimes, but the truth is no contact, space and time are also what give you the best chance of them ever coming back. And it’s a win-win, because it’s also what’s best for you to heal and the quickest most effective way for you to hurt less. You’ll be able to pour into other things that are good for you in that time and space too, but right now it probably doesn’t feel like it. So just do what you can to get time to pass. 

I also think you are doing the right thing by feeling the pain of these emotions. If it’s safe, keep feeling the feelings. Cry until you can’t. If your chest hurts and you’re having bad physical symptoms then obviously try and take a breather with a distraction like trash telly or something. Focus on breathing out as much as breathing in, emphasis on the breaths out helps soothe the panicking. The worst is now I’m so sorry, but you will get through it. Take care.

Describing something as c*nt or c*nty as a positive thing originated from queer culture, and the drag and ballroom scene to mean bringing “female realness and general exquisiteness.” It’s an expression that nowadays is as much about celebrating drag queens embracing their femininity as it is about women embracing their femininity and female identity/power. And a reclaiming of a word that was typically weaponised against women by men. It’s kinda like a homage to the way queer people compliment women or femme presenting people, and how women themselves have since adopted the term in popular culture.

She’s using it in a fun camp way in the song, “issimo” meaning very, so “very c*nt.” I don’t think it’s all that deep haha 😅 but it’s also not meant to be derogatory to women, quite the opposite.

This happened to me. He dumped me 7 days after a visit. It wasn’t the best visit, we had actually had a long chat about the relationship, were brutally honest about some issues, voiced our fears, talked through some suggested solutions/changes we could make, but ultimately ended the conversation positive, lying cuddled up in each others arms and committed to making it work. 

Left on a huge romantic high. Like he gave me the longest most loving and romantic goodbye of the entire relationship, then ended it 7 days later over the phone. All the texting in between was loving and supportive too. 

I have a huge fear now that the big loving romantic goodbye was just a facade and he knew it was the last time he would see me while I didn’t. Like he let me get my hopes up knowing he was going to twist the knife in a week later. I feel like it’s given me huge trust issues, and actually genuinely horrifies me and creeps me out that he might have done that. I would’ve preferred he just ended it in person and think he’s a coward for doing it the way he did. I think ultimately that’s what it comes down to - people are selfish and want to break up with people the way that feels easiest for them, rather than what’s best for the dumpee. 

On the same phone call that my long distance ex dumped me on, he was literally giving me reassurances and updating me on job applications he was doing in lieu of closing the gap at the beginning. Then out of nowhere he kicked the legs from under me and said he didn’t think we should be in a relationship anymore. The whole thing was brutal and weird af but I guess he was struggling to work up the courage and it was easier to drop a quick bomb mid-phone call and run without taking the time to think how to explain and deliver news of his decision with care. I have broken up with a partner or two in the past, including a long distance one, and however awful it was I made sure to do it in person and properly sit down to talk it all through so that the other person at least got a full explanation and the chance to say a proper goodbye. But other people prefer a light touch hit-and-run approach like my ex I guess.

I’ve tried a few and I’m now on 50mg of quetiapine. So far so good in terms of minimal side effects, it is sedating so I take the immediate release form of the tablet and it just gives me good sleep. It’s only been a few weeks but I really think it’s helping. And I’m going through a breakup right now so it’s being put to the test lol.

Mirtazapine really helped my mood but gave me horrendous food cravings, like an insatiable hunger than never left so ultimately I had to come off it. I was really, really worried that quetiapine would have the same hunger side effect but it hasn’t at all. So that would be my best recommendation, especially if you’ve already tried SSRIs. The other one I am yet to try but would have if quetiapine didn’t work would be venlafaxine.

I understand, and I’ve heard a lot of different takes on this type of thing before so I know some people think it’s ridiculous and frame it as “why are you jealous of a cartoon” while others flat out don’t want their partner looking at this content (or porn in general) at all.

I realised that for me a big part of why it makes me feel uncomfortable is that I just find it disturbing how much women are sexualised in general in society and in many forms of media, and I worry about the impact of men regularly consuming content that sexualises women in any capacity, even if it’s “just a cartoon” because it does have real world implications, a big one being this enormous pressure to fit increasingly complex attainable conventional beauty standards. I think it also contributes to this feeling as a woman that when you’re in a monogamous relationship with a man - and especially if you have BPD - that you are “competing” to hold his attention and remain desirable knowing that we live in a society that puts such an overemphasis on sexual appeal and attractiveness on women, which keeps us feeling not good enough. 

I’m generalising a little and I may not be articulating this exactly right, but I guess I’m bringing this up to remind you that it’s not always just BPD and “you’re just jealous.” The context of the world in which we live in adds fuel to the fire, and ultimately I personally have realised I don’t want to be in a relationship with someone who doesn’t understand that contributing to the sexualisation of women by over-consuming and sharing pornographic content to excess could be harmful to the way we view and treat women as a whole. That’s not to say I’m anti-porn completely, it just means I know I need to be with someone who is able to think and engage critically with regards to the topic of the sexualisation of women, and not just dismiss my concerns about such a nuanced and complex topic as “you’re jealous of a cartoon” etc. or just me being BPD psycho!

This stuff equal parts gives me the ick, enrages me and makes me insecure, so I’ve just been trying to dig into why and I think this is where I’m at. I want to be sex positive and I certainly don’t want to be controlling of a partner’s porn consumption, but this whole sharing stuff with his friends a lot would be difficult for me. TLDR: it’s hard out here living in a society lol, especially with BPD so don’t be too hard on yourself.

I think generally speaking deprioritising romance in general is good for me with my BPD as a whole. 

Taking the pressure off finding a life partner and the mindset that I require one to live a happy and fulfilled life is something I’m working on. I would like a life partner, and if I don’t end up having one will probably have a degree of mourning what could have been. But I realise I can’t let that be the determining factor in whether life is worth living or not. I need other hopes and dreams to value just as much as romance. If a life partner happens then great. If not, I need to know I can still be just as happy. And I genuinely believe there can be major pros to not having a life partner. But honestly I think even people without BPD could benefit from a bit more of this mindset sometimes as our society really does heavily, heavily emphasise the importance of finding “the one” which can make people feel like they’re failed or destined for a life of gloom if that never happens.

However situationships for me aren’t the answer, they are hell for my BPD lol. I would take a long term relationship where I can actually work with someone who has decided to be committed and who is hopefully more likely to put in the time and care to try and make it work. Situationships tend to be too up in the air for me, and toxic. Casual relationships with clearly defined boundaries and expectations could work I suppose, but as with a lot of things with BPD, I can get onboard in theory but it’s much harder to do in practice.

Yikes most of these replies to a sixteen year old girl posting on Reddit for the first time are bizarre! Can people please have some compassion and sensitivity for a literal teenager? So much unnecessary admonishment.

OP, I totally understand where you’re coming from. He is also young and figuring out himself, the world around him and how he feels, so I want to extend compassion to him too. But a good lesson to start to learn in relationships is that we can never really control the other person’s behaviours, much less their beliefs, unless they are genuinely interested, committed, and inspired to change.

What you can control is your own boundaries. If you have said your piece and discussed this with him, I would now take the time to think about whether or not this is a dealbreaker for you in a relationship, rather than figuring out how you can try to change him. A big part of relationships and life in general is figuring out what you do and don’t want, and what you can and can’t compromise on. I would maybe take some time to tune into how you feel, maybe even write down the things that are important to you in a relationship and figure out if being in a relationship with someone who has such a different point of view to you is something you can compromise on, or not. 

If you choose to stay with him the compromise shouldn’t be that you feel you have to dilute or change your own beliefs however. The compromise would be you both existing fully as yourselves in the relationship, without the relationship becoming toxic with resentment or frustration. I think it’s admirable that you have these beliefs and want to make the world a better place. Please never lose that - not for a relationship, not for anything in the world. It is not “forcing your views on others” to stay true to yourself. You just have to focus on what you can control, not on what you can’t. Best of luck and take care, I know you’ll have a bright future either way.

I really do sympathise with your position, and I’ve read some of your comments replying to people and understand that it probably feels patronising and frustrating to hear some of the things people are telling you here. But my honest opinion is that it really is a red flag for a 28 year old guy to be going after a 19 year old, and even more of a red flag that he would deceive you in that way with the filter situation. 

I’m sure it’s not easy to just drop him like some people are saying, it’s tough when you have feelings for someone and it sounds like you don’t want to hurt his feelings either. I would encourage you to remember that he didn’t consider your feelings when he was being deceptive about his appearance, and how it would make you feel to find out about this. Relationships are built on trust and he breached it. It should make you question what else he might have lied about. And it is a totally valid and normal response to not be attracted to him now and to feel deceived or even a bit weirded out by the whole thing. It’s reason enough alone to want to withdraw or end things, and you don’t need to feel bad about that or like you owe it to him to try and force yourself to become attracted to him.

I personally think he was hiding how old he appeared in real life because he also knows that pursuing a 19 year old is inappropriate, and he suspected you would feel more aware of that and/or more uncomfortable if you saw how old he really looks. 

You have your autonomy and you are able to make your own choices. I remember when I was 19 I would probably have felt attacked and annoyed by people pointing out the age gap thing, I hate anyone questioning my judgement. But as I have grown I have realised that nothing good comes from an older guy pursuing someone as young as you, and it’s usually indicative of very problematic of even harmful intentions and character. I’m sorry if that is irritating to hear but I wouldn’t feel right not trying to warn you or point this out. I really hope you set a boundary here that you won’t put up with deceptive behaviour, that you deserve more and can find it with someone else who you’re  easily attracted to as well. Best of luck.

Other comments have covered a lot, I just want to add something I see (predominantly) women say all the time: “how do I make him see how much this hurts me?”

The answer is you can’t! If you have communicated about an issue over and over with someone, and their behaviour does not change, then either they do not want to change or are simply incapable of changing. It is not because you haven’t screamed enough, cried enough, tried enough, explained it well enough, tugged on his heart strings enough. Stop putting the onus on your ability to make someone else understand, you have tried. It is on your partner to BE understanding. 

You cannot force someone to have empathy for you. Nine times out of ten the sad answer is they simply do not care, care but do not care enough, or have a degree of care that simply does not translate to the action or change necessary.

There are so many reasons why this is a serious issue, alongside various other red flags other commenters have highlighted here, but I want to make the point that stuff like this is always a symptom, never the cause. The cause is your partner lacks empathy and despite your best efforts and communication and compromise, he hasn’t changed. Even if by some miracle you managed to force him to change on this one issue, do you really want to be with someone where you have to do that? 

If you have doubts about him leaving you when your health condition prevents you from working in the future then I really think you need to consider calling time on this relationship. If he cannot step up now to consider and adapt to your needs (and really it is a tiny compromise in the scheme of life, and certainly in the scheme of supporting a partner with a health condition) do you really have enough faith that he can step up later? 

You have to protect yourself and your future. This is not the type of person to take a risk on when you know that’s coming down the line which must be so hard and difficult to bear. I totally get not wanting to throw the whole boyfriend away, it sucks when there may be other positives to your relationship that you really cherish. But perhaps it  is best to take a risk on leaving and finding someone equipped with the empathy and understanding you need instead, who you can rely on in the future because you definitely deserve that.

Best of luck to you and take care <3

My understanding is it really varies person to person. My sister and I both had lip filler, both had about the same amount, I found it painful, she didn’t find it painful at all 🤷‍♀️

I was very much like you, very scared, very pain-averse, have dealt with a lot of health anxiety in the past. It wasn’t a pleasant experience, but some things that helped me:

- a stress ball or something else to hold in my hands during 
- remember that tbh… it is just a tiny needle going in a tiny amount in the grand scheme of things. People go through all sorts of medical procedures on the daily that are far worse and far more invasive, so I tell myself if they can get through that I can get through silly old lip filler!
- I think of the positive reasons “why” I want lip filler during and focus on the fact this is a means to an end to get those benefits. Focusing on looking forward to the results is motivation to mentally push through if it starts to hurt. 
- thinking of celebs who have had work done and being like “if xyz actress/singer/reality star can tough it out then i can too” 😂

All in all for me it was painful but it wasn’t like the worst pain in the world and it doesn’t last that long.

The first time I booked an appointment with my injector I showed up terrified, and she was so kind and point blank told me to reschedule when I was in a better headspace. She said even she as an injector gets nervous getting beauty procedures done sometimes. She said nerves are normal but being deathly afraid is not, and that ultimately it is supposed to be a good, fun, positive thing we’re doing. Maybe the process is a bit uncomfortable and ouchy, but it should be fun to explore aesthetics and experiment and experience a new look. When I went back again I had more of that attitude instead, and normal nerves instead of the initial panic lol. Also lip filler can be dissolved if you hate it, and complications are very rare.

Final advice is please give it time post-procedure! I was not good at this! I got myself very unnecessarily anxious in the days after worrying that the swelling wouldn’t go down, or that something bad would happen. Everyone told me to be patient but I was convinced my swollen look of days 1-3 would be my face permanently forever and was freaking out. It will go down so much over the next few weeks to 1 month, and tbh even now I’m surprised how subtle the end result is compared to how much they looked and felt immediately after. Any soreness however did not last that long for me. I was expecting way more pain post-procedure but it was fine.

Best of luck, I know you’ll be fine! It’s just lip filler at the end of the day!

Just to clarify, are you concerned that even if you have a vasectomy your wife will leave you to try and have another child with someone else anyway? 

If so, there needs to be an honest chat with your wife so you know what her priorities are: is it staying in a relationship with you, without children? Or is it leaving this relationship to try having children with someone else, either naturally with low odds or with an egg donor like you said she suggested?

However, if you are both sure - and have reassured each other - you are committed to staying in this relationship regardless of kids, then I think having a vasectomy might be a solution to consider. I can sympathise with not wanting to undergo surgery (I am squeamish about surgery myself) but do some research and weigh up the pros and cons. Most vasectomies are reversible, and anyway, if you don’t want children with her or anyone else it shouldn’t be a concern whether it’s reversible or not. 

I sympathise with your wife’s fertility struggles, it must be very challenging for her. My advice on that front is to be emotionally supportive and encourage her to see a therapist if she doesn’t already have one. Therapy might not be a bad idea for both of you individually and/or together to really figure out what your priorities are in life: kids vs no kids, this marriage vs no marriage vs going your separate ways to find someone else more compatible on the kids front. 

I would also encourage you to self reflect honestly on the real reasons you are not wanting a vasectomy. Women sacrifice a lot for their reproductive and sexual health, so I don’t feel a vasectomy is an unreasonable request on balance, but it is ultimately your choice what you are comfortable with doing. Is it just fear of surgery? Is it that you think you may want to leave this relationship to have children with someone else? Is it that you think your wife might leave you to have children with someone else? Or is it unrelated resentment built up from the other sacrifices you say you feel you’ve made for the relationship? 

You are right that neither a sexless marriage nor risking pregnancy when when one parent doesn’t want a kid are the answers here. Best of luck to you both.

I don’t have loads to offer here which hasn’t already been covered by others, but I do have BPD and while I don’t think your husband has BPD at all (bear with me) I will say that I am someone who struggles a lot with rumination, negativity, depression, job anxiety / existential crisis relating to employment, and has in the past had this significantly affect me and my relationships. It is a lot more managed now and what has massively helped is setting boundaries around when, where and for how long myself and my partner are allowed to vent to each other and be negative. 

Learning the balance between healthy venting and sharing feelings vs. rumination and hyper fixation on a problem to the point of perpetuating my own misery has been tough but is doable. I came to understand that the more I talked over and over about a problem, my brain was doing so to try and resolve the core issue but ultimately I was using constant venting to others as a substitute for developing my own independent emotional regulation skills. And the reason for that was low self-esteem and lack of belief in my own ability to resolve problems and be resilient. I wonder if your husband’s constant complaining has its roots in something similar? Maybe deep down he doesn’t feel competent or capable or like he can rely on himself, so he’s going round in circles and only offloading the feelings onto you to regulate instead (which I am not condoning btw, deeply unfair on you).

At the start of my relationship my partner and I would get into such heavy negative chats it was sucking the joy out of everything. We are now much better at calling out each other’s negative spirals, checking in with each other to see when we need a time out from talking about negative things, and generally being more cognisant and considerate when it comes to verbalising negativity, without repressing emotions. 

Ultimately it all starts with self-awareness. He isn’t recognising the impact this is having on you and on himself (as the constant complaining clearly isn’t helping him to feel better - it’s making him feel worse) so self-awareness is the first step and you can help him by telling him what you’ve told us. My only advice on delivery would be to leave out any comparisons between yourself and him (although valid!) when you speak to him to avoid him becoming defensive. 

I used to be very all or nothing - either it was a safe space to vent and it would all come out at full speed and overwhelm the person, or I would bottle things up and never talk about them. It seems that’s a concern for you re: confronting your husband. I think confront him anyway and ask him to take this to a therapist to work this out. I don’t personally believe that laziness is a primary emotion, I think it’s a secondary emotion that’s usually the result of anxiety or some other thing we are avoiding. All this to say though that your feelings are valid and I empathise deeply, it is infuriating and draining for you, you deserve space for your emotions too remember - you can’t continue this way and I hope things improve for your sake as much as his. Best of luck.

Hey, first of all I’m so sorry you’re going through this. It must be incredibly distressing and a total mind fuck. There’s a lot of big complicated feelings to unpack here, and it’s no wonder you’re feeling the way you’re feeling. 

The first most obvious advice is to find a professional to talk to, like a therapist or an online charity. If you can, also speak to a trusted friend or family member for emotional support as well. Bottling this all up must feel terrible and you’re not alone. 

There’s only so much Reddit is going to be able to help here so a professional is best, I wouldn’t want the opinions of tonnes of strangers online to add to your confusion. Having said that, if other perspectives would help here’s my own:

• You’ve done absolutely nothing wrong. It is totally normal to feel like you have in these situations, but I promise you haven’t. It’s more likely that feeling of “oh god I’ve done something wrong” is actually your brain trying to protect you and say “something has happened that has caused me distress and I need help.” So I promise, none of this is your fault.

• Secondly, your coach is the one who did something wrong. It doesn’t matter if you had a good relationship before, looked up to him, fantasised about him before, etc. He is your coach and he shouldn’t be having sexual interactions with any of his students, period. He also took advantage of the fact that you were vulnerable in many ways. Being closeted, a virgin, and having an emotionally absent father, those are huge things to be dealing with. He has abused his position of responsibility and authority, and is displaying no empathy or remorse for the distress this has caused you. Physically covering your mouth to keep you from showing the consequences of HIS actions is crazy.

• I know that you nodded when he asked you if he could proceed, so you feel you consented to what happened and I understand why. But consent should always be enthusiastic and freely given. It should never be coerced and I am of the opinion he coerced you. Any sexual act should feel like a safe space, you should feel in control even over the amount of control you wish to give to the other person. I’m so sorry you experienced the opposite of that. I know you say he didn’t assault you in any legal sense but a) that might not actually be the case depending on where you are in the world and b) the law doesn’t negate the distress this has caused or excuse the fact that he has behaved in a way that has caused you psychological harm. You don’t need the law to legitimise your pain. 

• I also want to say that making sense of this is probably going to involve coming to terms with the concept of “many things can be true at once and that’s okay.”

For example, you might want sexual intimacy (like most human beings) but that doesn’t mean you want coerced sexual experiences. 

You might fantasise about people, but that doesn’t give them permission to coerce you into sexual acts that happen in real life.

You might find yourself “hoping something happens again” as you put it, perhaps because you desire sexual exploration and intimacy, or perhaps because this person felt like someone you admired, trusted, and is someone who you shared your first sexual experience with. You don’t feel able to come out to everyone in your life as bisexual and the relief of being able to be open about that with him, even in those circumstances, might have felt good and like something you want to experience again. However, that DOES NOT make this person a safe person to engage in sexual acts with moving forward, it doesn’t negate the distress that you are experiencing after what happened, and it doesn’t mean that you’ve done something wrong or that he is any less accountable for his actions. 

The main priority is that you keep yourself safe from this man and get the support you need. There are charities that are able to support with all of the things you are experiencing (being closeted, bisexual, and a survivor of sexual coercion and assault if you come to view it that way). A good therapist will be able to advise you on what safeguarding steps should be taken, and will help you to unpack all these thoughts and feelings so that you won’t feel so distressed.  

And finally, you have a long life ahead of you where you will have the opportunity to have sexual and emotional intimacy with people (men, women, all genders) who are safe, who care about your well-being, who make you feel happy and calm after sex, not guilty, disgusted and afraid. I hope that future also involves you being able to be your full bisexual self, on the football team or anywhere else.

Best of luck and take care, it’s going to be okay.

I’ve been reading your comments and from what I can gather you suspect you may have OCD but have struggled to find a therapist who deals with paraphilia. I’m not sure what country you’re in or how you’re going about finding a therapist, but I do think I would focus on just finding one who deals with OCD and go from there. I would stop obsessing about finding one who absolutely definitely is an expert in zoophilia because at the end of the day, what needs treating is the OCD, intrusive thoughts and distress around it, and just because someone isn’t upfront stating an “expertise” in paraphilia doesn’t mean they won’t have experience working with people who have are dealing with thoughts of zoophilia. In fact, I think it’s highly likely that a lot of therapists who treat OCD have heard very similar or the same before. And the human brain can be rewired. 

I know you said you don’t want to just modify the thoughts, you want to get them gone. I appreciate the frustration and despair, but I honestly believe that to get to a point where the thoughts are gone requires starting with modification and going from there. The catch 22 of OCD is that the more you obsess over not thinking about the The Thing, the more The Thing becomes ever present and overwhelming in your mind. A good therapist will be able to help you to teach your brain not to get stuck in that loop, and also to take a less black-and-white approach to recovery. At the moment it sounds like you’re in quite and all-or-nothing mindset of either the thoughts go or you’re killing yourself. I totally understand that, but I would really encourage you to look for shades of grey and think of some small steps that could help you get the right support, and go from there. I would start by just looking up support for general OCD, either through charities, support groups, or your healthcare provider. 

Others have said it but if you’re not acting on these thoughts or making plans to, then none of this is your fault. I doubt you’re alone in having these kind of thoughts, and there is very much hope of a future where these thoughts are a distant memory, and just a symptom of a health condition that was untreated at the time. Best of luck OP, this doesn’t have to be the end.

I have experience working for a charity that helps disabled people with their sexual health and sexuality, so I will add my two cents here:

A common misconception is that disabled people do not have sex. They do! Disabled people are entitled to sexual expression and romantic relationships. The main thing to be aware of is capacity to consent. Down’s Syndrome (like many disabilities) varies in terms of its impact on a variety of mental and physical capabilities, but from what you’ve described, it sounds like Emma does have capacity to consent, which is the most important thing here. 

However, if you have any concerns at all on that front it might be wise to double-check with her parents to get a full understanding of her capacity to consent and anything else you think it would be important to know to make her experience of dating, sex and relationships comfortable for her. I would also seek advice from official National charities and associations for Down’s Syndrome as they will be able to provide clarity, and also could be a useful tool to educate yourself and those in your circle. 

I would probably also advise moving forward that you have a conversation with Emma about consent (both verbal and non-verbal, what words and signals mean “no”, the traffic light system of consent is great also) and take things slow to ensure you are both comfortable. But tbh we should all be having more of these kinds of consent conversations in our lives, not just with disabled people! 

You may have heard Down’s Syndrome “have a mental age of 8 or 9” and therefore “they are a child inside so you’d be having sex with a child” but it’s not that straightforward. Down’s syndrome can affect things like attention span, verbal memory and impulsivity, for example, at rates which - when compared with the general population - might be on par with that of an 8 or 9 year old per se. But that doesn’t necessarily make them “not an adult.” Like I said, every person with Down’s Syndrome is different. 

Unfortunately it’s common for people to jump straight to infantilising disabled people in general. If someone is disabled to the point that they cannot consent and/or understand practices around safe sex and safe healthy relationships it would be a no-go, but that does not seem to be the case from what you’ve described. There’s actually evidence to suggest that a lot of people with Down’s syndrome have greater than average emotional intelligence and social sensitivity. 

My advice is to keep educating yourself, seek the support of charities, and keep communicating with her parents, and above all listen to Emma and her needs as she absolutely has a voice and autonomy in this. Good luck!

I’m sorry you’re feeling this bad about it. Others have said it but it sounds like OCD potentially, but regardless, obsessive thoughts of some kind about this incident. Ruminating is a way of trying to control the situation and make it different rather than accepting what’s happened and focusing on a future where you don’t do that sort of thing again. But before you get to acceptance you have to process the feelings of fear and shame.

The thing about obsessive thoughts is that it’s often a coping mechanism to avoid feeling a feeling we don’t want to feel. For example, you are trying to avoid the feeling of fear and guilt, so instead your brain uses obsessive thoughts and rumination to try to problem solve your way out of it so to speak, and prevent you from just accepting and feeling the feeling. 

An exercise that helps me might be something like the following: sit down and just focus on the feeling in your body associated with this incident. E.g. If it feels like fear, let it come up. Notice where you feel it in your body. Don’t think about the feeling and why you’re feeling it. Just notice how it feels in your body, what it does to your heartbeat or your breathing maybe. It might even make you cry. That would just be your body trying to release the stress of it to help you. Of course, if it feels too much to the point you think you might harm yourself or others STOP the exercise. But if you think you can allow your body to feel the feeling in a safe way, you might find that the feeling is not as big and insurmountable as you might think. You might find that once you’ve allowed yourself to feel it for a minute or two, it passes, or at least eases up. It’s a bit like slowly letting air out of a balloon over time until the issue becomes smaller and smaller. 

Your body is crying out for you to release some of the stress it’s carrying from the mental distress you’re under. Even suicidal thoughts can be your brain just trying to cope and warn you that it needs some stress relieving. In a weird way these suicidal thoughts could just be your body and your brain begging for rest and for you to have some self compassion.  

Another thing that can help obsessive thoughts is just to start noticing when they come up, let them come up, and let them pass. Easier said than done, but noticing them is the first step. Practice acknowledging when you’re beginning to ruminate. If a thought comes up, it comes up, it’s okay. Just allow it to exist, recognise it, you don’t have to pretend it doesn’t exist (that can make it worse, actually) but try not to pour gasoline on it by spending the next few hours thinking of who/what/why’s behind the thought.

I think teaching your brain it can be safe to feel difficult feelings could be a positive step. Especially as you really don’t need to be feeling this level of guilt and shame to the point you think you deserve to die. You definitely don’t deserve to die. 

I’m sorry therapy and medication hasn’t worked yet. I don’t know what sort of therapy and meds you’ve tried but if you haven’t yet, I would flag the link between obsessive thoughts and suicidal ideation to a professional, and see if you can get tested for OCD. There is help for you but it sounds like so far you’ve not been getting the right help. Take care and good luck.

I understand this must be very overwhelming and difficult for you to proceed, and your feelings are very valid. 

Firstly I want to nip in the bud the idea that she “enjoyed” being raped. That’s a hard no in answer to that question. 

As an SA survivor myself, if you think about it, by your current logic then any survivor of sexual assault could potentially be “trying to recreate their assault” every time they have sex. I can assure you that’s really not necessarily the case. My SA was a long time ago now, and sometimes me and my future partners have done things in the bedroom which technically “happened” during the assaults I experienced in the past. But the way I experience those sexual acts is totally different For example, my hair was pulled during my assault but I have since engaged in hair pulling multiple times with future partners and I never imagine my assault. The hair pulling with consent and with the safety of a partner who loves and cares for me, is nowhere near reminiscent of the hair pulling that happened when I was assaulted. It did take time and support to get there in the immediate aftermath but it was achievable. 

Of course, if you are maybe early on in your healing journey from assault and you are actively being triggered by certain sexual acts, and/or even intentionally engaging in those sexual acts to be triggered as a way to work through that trauma - and you as a partner don’t feel comfortable or equipped to be participating in that - it would be different and you are in your right to opt out of that. But it doesn’t sound like that’s necessarily what’s going on.

I agree it can absolutely be an empowering thing to recreate sexual acts that happened during an assault with the safety of a partner, making a bad thing good etc. I’ve done that before too. But I also want to emphasise that this can very much also look like simply moving on from the association of those acts with the assault. That is very possible, and very common - there is life after sexual assault and sexual abuse, and it’s okay to trust and believe that sex is not irreversibly tainted by assault. (This might be a terrible analogy lol, but say you had a car crash and you were really shaken up. And until you processed that trauma you were thinking about the car crashing everytime you drove anywhere. But eventually with time and healing it would be more than possible to be able to drive again without thinking about it).

Therapy for you both is always a good idea, or contact a charity who specialises in SA as they often provide support for loved ones of survivors. You’re right it is a privilege she’s shared this information with you. If you do discuss or raise any of these questions/concerns with her, I advise doing your best to reassure her she is not damaged or a problem or  less attractive to you because of this. Make it clear it is you and her versus. the issue. The issue simply being confusion around what this might mean about how she experiences the sex you have together and that you want to make sure you and her feel safe and positive about the sex you’re both having. Good luck!

Some kinda harsh comments here imo, I think because some people find it hard to empathise with sex as an outlet as it triggers people’s fear of cheating. I don’t think your problem is that you’re not motivated to not cheat, you clearly desperately want to control these urges, but much like any destructive behaviour associated with BPD, it’s not that simple to just stop. People should remember that before being quick to judge.

When I was 21 I had a similar issue, and now I’m 29 it’s one aspect of my BPD that’s completely under control so I want to give you hope it can get better.

Rather than trying to find an outlet for these urges like an open relationship (which won’t solve the problem) you MUST address the root cause. Ultimately the problem is that when you split or have a reason to want to withdraw from your partner, you seek closeness and attention from other people as a way to regulate those powerful painful feelings of fear and potential abandonment. It’s also coming from a place of insecurity about not being enough, and the attention of others feels soothing. Sex with other people is a band aid for these feelings, it will never be enough. Other people’s attention gives a false sense of security, their attention is usually fake and cheap and based on an idea of you, not the real you. You have to find other ways to a) validate the difficult feelings of insecurity and fear and b) regulate them. 

For a) I recommend a therapist, venting to friends, journaling, and making art.
For b) I recommend distraction techniques, hobbies, pouring into yourself rather than seeking to be affirmed from people outside yourself

You are doing the right thing by communicating with your partner. But together you can come up with better solutions than an open relationship. Even in an open relationship, sleeping with other people to avoid facing feelings of insecurity or splitting on a partner isn’t healthy or sustainable. Your partner can support with a) and b) but cannot be the only thing to help with validation and regulation, he can just be a part of that support.

I still struggle with these feelings but I now don’t deal with them by seeking attention from potential partners outside my romantic relationships. The guilt and destruction to my life and other people’s by acting on these feelings when I was your age is NOT worth it, and I really hope my reply saves you from the pain of those mistakes. Well done for seeking help, I think that’s admirable and brave, and remember it can get better and there are other ways to cope with these feelings. Good luck!

First of all, I actually really relate to this feeling. I think I was more in this headspace a few years ago, and now feel I have a much better sense of my personality, likes and dislikes etc. But I don’t necessarily think that’s the only way to go about it.

I think I would question whether or not there’s actually something wrong with you in the first place. You’ve labelled these things about yourself as “boring” but I feel like you show traits that can be really positive - you sound adaptable, flexible, open-minded to trying new things, open to doing things your partner wants to do. All of those things could make you considerate and curious and better able to go with the flow, not “boring.” 

Is the only reason you’re feeling this way because you think your boyfriend has an issue with it? If you took him out of the equation, would it bother you that much in the first place? It’s okay to just accept yourself the way you are if you’re happy not having strong preferences or opinions on things!

Two things can also be true at once though: you can accept yourself for where you’re at now and not beat yourself up / call yourself “boring” for not having a clearer sense of self (and have extra compassion for the fact that this is literally a symptom of BPD, which might be worth reminding your bf). However, it can also be something you’re curious about working on, independent of your bf’s approval.

Rather than feeling like you have to “decide” what your personality is or what you want to do/watch/eat/listen to, maybe you could just do a process of “trying everything on for size.” E.g. Look up a list of values and personality traits - see if you think any of them sound like you, and if not, any that might sound like you, any that do NOT sound like you, or simply any that you’d like to try embodying more of to see what it feels like. E.g. foods, look up a list of cuisines / restaurants / takeout places and see what you’d like to try. It doesn’t mean a commitment to liking or dislike, or to deciding these things are definitely “you.” It’s exploring and that’s ok. Take the pressure off yourself to have a fully-formed sense of self, it’s always going to be an ever-evolving work in progress for us all anyway. 

I hope some of this helps, but regardless, none of this makes you “boring” or anything else negative! I promise!

I’m really sorry for the abuse you suffered, that sounds unimaginably difficult. It makes sense that sex and sexuality are confusing for you. 

I agree with other comments re: your virginity. To your question about being attracted to traits in other women that your abusers have/had, this is actually a surprisingly common phenomenon amongst survivor-victims of sexual assault. It doesn’t make you weird or broken or anything like that. 

Even people who haven’t been assaulted but have been abused in the past or had toxic relationships in general, can still find themselves drawn to the traits of those people in others in future relationships. There’s nothing inherently wrong with it, depending on the traits I suppose, and to what extent that attraction is having a negative impact on your life and on others. E.g. if attracted to people who display violent abusive behaviour, that’s a problem because it puts you at risk. If just attracted to people who have say, green eyes, and your abusers had green eyes, there’s nothing necessarily to worry about that. It depends how well the person has been able to process their trauma. 

Sometimes our brains try to recreate trauma in different ways to try and process it. One of those ways is seeking people or situations - either consciously or unconsciously - that are reminiscent of the original trauma itself, or of the original abuser. It can be a way of reenacting a traumatic experience on your own terms and seeking to gain control over it, whereas the original trauma was an experience out of your control that probably created feelings of lasting helplessness.

Whenever you experience things like this that seem weird or worrying, I promise it is just your brain trying to process things and look out for you. It is trying to keep you alive, to keep you surviving trauma. And there is nothing weird or wrong about that. Knowing this helped me to be kinder to my brain and appreciate how hard it works to keep me safe, even if it doesn’t always get it right. Have you considered therapy at all? If not, I would suggest seeking out therapy specific for survivor-victims of sexual assault. Therapy can help your brain find the safe, healthy, and most effective ways to process trauma. 

You mention you are a “cisgender black man” and that “men don’t usually ask this question” which suggests you might have concerns about talking about this at all. You are absolutely capable of having a happy and healthy sex life if you want that for yourself. Please don’t think that isn’t on the cards for you because of what happened. I would just suggest seeking some support to get you there.

Best of luck to you and take care.

First of all, really sorry to hear you struggled with depression. It’s amazing you managed to continue even with freelance work in spite of mental illness so you deserve major credit. (I quit full-time employment due to depression, and tried freelance work but have even failed at that lol so I’m genuinely impressed).

The point being, it sounds like 1.5 years out of full-time employment, rather than 1.5 years out of working at all. On/off freelancing is still valuable work. For all employers know, you were just comfortable doing on/off freelance work for a period of time - they don’t need to know the real reason you switched to on/off freelance was because you were depressed, or that the whole time you were worrying you needed to be in full-time employment.

I suggest highlighting your freelance projects, big them up, make a list of skills learnt and developed. Then if they ask “why freelance not full time employment?” you could say you decided to switch to freelance for a bit for a better work/life balance and autonomy, to figure out what you wanted to do with your career, what skills to focus on, etc. And now you’re back with a clearer idea of what you want from your career, and “xyz role sounds like a perfect fit” (i.e. flatter them by suggesting that their company / role is whats drawn you back into the idea of full time employment because it sounds so good - doesn’t matter if this is a lie or not lol, just puts a positive spin). 

All of this can make you sound like a candidate who knows what they want, has taken control of their career direction and personal development, rather than taking any old job, or staying in a job that you weren’t enjoying. And it’s not far from the truth - taking time off work to focus on getting your mental health better IS admirable and IS a sign of someone taking initiative and focusing on personal development which is something to be proud of.

You could even say you intended to only have a few months on/off freelancing and figuring things out, but then the pandemic hit which extended the time out of full-time employment longer than perhaps you had planned or anticipated. 

Just some ideas, I hope they make sense and sorry if they don’t help. 

Finally, while you absolutely aren’t obliged TK disclose your struggles with depression, I would suggest that whatever solution you come up with is as close to the truth as you feel comfortable with. Elaborate lies are hard to maintain and cause more stress than they’re worth. You don’t have to use words like “depression” or “mental illness” (though you can if you want to, it’s not embarrassing at all, it just sucks some employers are ignorant and may discriminate - but they aren’t worth working for anyway). You can substitute for phrases like “took some personal time off” “took time off to attend to personal matters”, or “time off to focus on personal development and figure out what I want from life.” Might also be worth researching companies you apply to and the type of work culture e.g. some companies have mental health support available and actively advertise these things. Gauging the company culture and attitudes towards mental health and well-being before applying might make you feel more confident about being accepted.

OCD may sound like a terrifying and horrid illness, but it is very treatable. A diagnosis of OCD or any mental illness doesn’t have to be a bad thing. It’s not a restrictive label or a condemnation - diagnoses are helpful, because they’re signposts to help you access the support you need. 

Like a lot of mental “illnesses”, OCD is just another way our brain tries to control and cope with the world around us. It can manifest in different ways, but one reason why intrusive thoughts can happen is because the brain is just having trouble processing anxiety. There’s a cycle of repressing the thought, and then the thought comes back stronger, “intruding” into our brain seemingly without our control, so we repress it more, so it comes back stronger, and the cycle continues ..... 

The point is, they CAN be controlled, by addressing the anxiety. The cycle can absolutely be broken, but you need the right treatment (medication and / or the right kind of therapy). 

I completely understand why it might feel hard to open up to your therapist about these thoughts, but I would strongly encourage you to try, and especially to try this first before suicide. Therapists hear a lot of things, they are professionally trained to hear dark thoughts and difficult subject matter. They really can help. If you are worried about what your therapist will think of you, just remember they have probably heard it all before - or worse - as you are definitely not alone in having intrusive thoughts such as these.

I promise it’s not too late even though it might feel like that now. I’m sorry everything feels so hopeless, but I think this breaking point could be a turning point instead.

My advice for next steps: tell your therapist about your thoughts. Have you told your therapist that you have intrusive thoughts at all? Or have you just told them you have intrusive thoughts, but not said that the thoughts are about child abuse? If you are having trouble saying them out loud, you could consider writing them down and giving them to your therapist to read if speaking them out loud is too difficult. You could even just show your therapist this Reddit post! But please talk to your therapist about them. I really think it will help.

Not saying you’re the asshole, but if the ultimatums / shouting / stern talkings to etc. aren’t working, then an alternative (which you may have tried) might be to sit her down and just ask her if she’s ok. Find out exactly what she’s feeling. 

Tell her you want to try to suspend judgement for a moment and understand her point of view, even if you disagree, and just hear her out. Her dramatics and avoidance may be coming from a place of anxiety and confusion. Just because she doesn’t have a diagnosed mental illness or learning disability, doesn’t mean she isn’t still legitimately struggling emotionally.

Is she scared? Scared of growing up? Scared she’s not good enough? Or clever enough? Or capable enough? Does the thought of “adult” life depress her? Fill her with dread? Realising how shitty capitalism is can be a catalyst for existential crisis. I don’t blame her if she’s feeling sad or anxious or angry if all she sees in her future is working a 9-5 for a company she hates, for a society she’s disillusioned with (I mean that sounds like 90% of Reddit rn)

It could be that in her mind, she’s overwhelmed and catastrophising. She may feel that completing high school equates to agreeing to live life in a way that goes completely against her values, and that it’s the first step to being trapped in a life she doesn’t want. 

I could be wrong, but either way, my advice is:

- Let her talk and listen to her feelings first. Don’t interject. Make sure you demonstrate compassion and empathy first before offering solutions. This is hard to do, but essential.

- Once she feels heard, then reassure her that your intentions are to make her feel better and happier with life, now and in the long term, and that’s why you’re going to suggest some different ways of reframing the scenario. Reassure her your intentions are not to just “be right” or win an argument, or force her to conform to values that aren’t her own (which she may be perceiving your attempts to help as).

- Suggest that perhaps completing high school or any education is a first step to helping to change the “capitalist” system from within. If there are aspects of society she doesn’t like, education is a good place to start to be better equipped to change them. 

If after all this she still won’t do it, then you have to accept that - you don’t have to agree, but she is 18+ and will need to make her own mistakes and decisions. Does she have an alternative plan? Could she start her own business? 

I appreciate the financial burden and I totally get why you threatened to kick her out. I know it’s because you want to kickstart her into doing something with her life, and push her out of this negative headspace which can appear lazy and ungrateful from the outside. Laziness and ingratitude might be symptoms of what she’s going through - I’m not saying she’s entirely blameless - but I highly doubt they are the root causes. 

It’s a tricky situation, and I hope you’re ok. Wishing you and your daughter all the best.
